Anhydrides are highly reactive compounds that readily react with nucleophiles like amines. When anhydrides react with amines, they undergo nucleophilic acyl substitution reactions that form amide bonds. This reaction is typically exothermic (releases heat) and can be quite vigorous or even violent, especially with more reactive anhydrides and primary amines.

The reaction proceeds as follows:
1. The nucleophilic nitrogen atom of the amine attacks one of the carbonyl carbon atoms in the anhydride
2. This leads to the formation of an amide and a carboxylic acid
3. The reaction releases energy in the form of heat (exothermic)

Due to the high reactivity of anhydrides and the substantial energy release, these reactions can be violent if not properly controlled, especially with lower molecular weight anhydrides and amines.
